subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   FINANCIAL INSTITUTIONS ADVISABILITY OF INFORMING DEPOSITORS WHEN DEPOSITS ARE UNINSURED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the motion was last before the House on February 29, I was dealing with the current problem in the Province of Alberta where the Code Commission has been looking very seriously at the problems created by the Principal Group of companies for citizens right across the country.
That group of companies was composed of one company, Principal Trust, which was supervised by the Department of Insurance here. Bob Hammond was our Superintendent of Insurance. He is now the Deputy Superintendent of Financial Institutions. He was on top of that trust company starting back in 1983. However, the group of companies had several other emanations. In other words, there was a mutual company, a real estate company and various classes of investment companies in the securities field, all of which were generally categorized as Principal companies.
My friend, the Hon. Member for Kamloops-Shuswap (Mr. Riis) has put this motion after looking at the problems that developed in the Principal matter. He suggests that we make sure that everyone signs a piece of paper, as if people signing a piece of paper will, all of a sudden, bring about the great nirvana. You and I know, Mr. Speaker, what happens when people sign pieces of paper that they have not read. We would not have had the inquiry we have just completed, or in the process of getting ready to report, with respect to bank service charges, if people who dealt with banks read their agreement with the bank on opening an account in which they agreed that the bank could charge them anything it wanted to. That became the agreement, and that is the express agreement, and any changes were perfectly all right because they agreed to it. To give some person a piece of paper where they agree they are not insured by Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation is just so much drivel in terms of something to stop the abuse or problem.
The problem can be stopped, and would have been stopped and will be stopped, if we are able to get rid of competing regulations in this country. Right now the Government of
Financial Institutions
Canada supervises trust companies generally in most parts of the country through the Superintendent of Financial Institutions, but the Government of Canada does not supervise mutual funds or investment funds or co-op funds, that kind of thing. Who supervises them? Provincial supervisors, and the provincial people in Alberta knew about the problems because our people told them about the problems, but they did not do anything about it. They allowed, by their lack of regulation and supervision, by their attitude toward supervision, those problems to develop in the Principal Group.
The fact that someone signs something is not going to help. It is getting a sense of supervision that is the same across the country, a standard requirement of management across the country. That is the answer. That was the answer presented to this House in the report of the Standing Committee on Finance that reported on the Green Paper in November of 1985. It called for a national supervisory agency. The Hon. Member for Kamloops-Shuswap was part of that committee.
I am sure the Hon. Member remembers that particular discussion of the kinds of problems we were then faced with and with which we are faced today and with which we will continue to be faced as long as we have the supervision of financial institutions all over the place. There is a necessity for having unified supervision. That is the only way we can come to grips with the problem.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   FINANCIAL INSTITUTIONS ADVISABILITY OF INFORMING DEPOSITORS WHEN DEPOSITS ARE UNINSURED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened to the Hon. Chairman of the Finance Committee, and while I would agree with him that there is a need for co-ordinating regulations across Canada, that they probably need to be dealt with on the level of regulations, I cannot agree when he suggests that the motion put forward by my colleague, the Hon. Member for Kamloops Shuswap (Mr. Riis), would not be a very helpful addition to the regulations as they now stand. If this proposed amendment had been in place it would have prevented some of the heartache and financial tragedy we have seen in the last few years, particularly with the collapse of the Principal Group.
I want to commend my colleague, the Hon. Member for Kamloops-Shuswap, for bringing this motion forward. One of the most difficult things, as you know, Mr. Speaker, with which a Member of Parliament deals are constituents who lay out a case that clearly indicates they are innocent victims, that through no fault of their own, they are victims of some situation that has left them drained of their life savings. I met with one such couple and had them write a letter detailing their experience with the Principal Group. The husband was a recent immigrant. They were people who worked hard and saved because they saw their savings as the future for their children. I would like to read part of the letter this woman wrote: It says:
All our money was invested in First Investors Corporation, a member of the Principal Group. Every last penny my husband and I have earned and saved all these years through hard work and budgeting, even my children's family allowances and birthday gifts are involved. We have been working and saving for the future, for a good education and better opportunities for our children,

April 25, 1988
Financial Institutions
and now we have nothing to show for all those years and hard work. It hurts so much each time I think about it.
We had a total of approximately $200,000 in various accounts, including RRSPs. Now we have nothing but the weak assurances that some of the money (our own money) will be returned to us eventually.
We invested our moneys with the First Investors Corporation because we were repeatedly told by their agents,... that the moneys were 104 per cent guaranteed. We asked each time we invested and were told each time that if anything ever happened we were guaranteed 100 per cent refund plus 4 per cent interest. On the back of each contract we signed is written "Under the Investment Corporation Act (Alberta), assets equal to 100 per cent of certificate liabilities are maintained on deposit with a Canadian chartered bank".
Where were the government people who are supposed to check on these companies to see if they are abiding by the rules? Why were these people allowed to mislead their clients? Why wasn't closer watch kept on these institutions?
While I can agree with the previous speaker that we need to clean up the regulatory framework all across Canada to bring some kind of co-ordination and a systemizing to that framework, I also think that had the motion presented by my hon. colleague been in effect, people like my constituents, who received assurances time after time after time that their investments were firmly secured by insurance, having to read it and sign it, would not have been in the position in which they now find themselves.
In my constituency I had a great many teachers who had invested at different times in the B.C. Teachers' Investment and Housing Co-operative. This began back in 1951 as a small group of teachers who decided that a good way in which they could help one another to buy houses was to put some of their money into a housing co-operative that would allow other teachers to draw out of it and thus get a downpayment and their mortgage moneys. Over a period of time this housing cooperative expanded and went into other markets. It kind of grew like Topsy without people always being fully aware of what was involved. Like so many other institutions in western Canada it became involved in some real estate transactions. When the real estate market fell apart in western Canada the B.C. Teachers' Investment and Housing Co-operative suffered. In 1985 it had to go into receivership. These people were lucky to get a few cents on the dollar. They lost very substantially. Some of them, again, had put almost their total life savings into this one co-operative. Others had more of a mix.
Mrs. Lillian Holeton, who is the Chair of the special committee appointed by the B.C. Retired Teachers' Association, made a submission to the Standing Committee on Finance and Economic Affairs. She pointed out that the question of insurance or guarantee has been constantly apparent since the federal Government instituted legislation in 1967, that is, the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation Act, covering deposit insurance for banks and trust companies, while the provincial Government enacted similar legislation covering some trust companies and credit unions.
The B.C. Teachers' Investment and Housing Co-operative made overtures to the provincial Government in 1977, 1978 and 1979 up to and into its insolvency in January of 1986 asking that the question of its status and insurance guarantee position be clarified. There was no response to these requests on the basis that the Teachers' Investment and Housing Cooperative by its formation did not fall under any current legislation.
Here again we have a situation in which people were concerned to try to get information about the insurance status of their organization. They were not given any kind of clarification. When the market collapsed and it reverberated back to the Investment and Housing Co-operative, it was placed in receivership. These people lost a great deal of their investment.
Again, as I said, some teachers who had been working hard all their lives and trying to save for their retirement lost their total life savings. I know some of these people. Some were already retired and they lost substantially from their life savings.
The motion put forward by the Hon. Member for Kamloops-Shuswap is something very simple. It is that the federal Government, in co-operation with the provinces, institute a regime by which federal and provincial Governments would require that whenever anybody made a deposit that would not be covered by insurance, they would have to sign a waiver clearly indicating that this was so. Obviously, there are some people who, seeing the possibility of perhaps greater gains at greater interest rates would want to take a chance and invest even when there is no insurance. That is their choice. It should be a matter of choice. It should not be a matter of deception. If they choose to invest when there is no insurance, they know that they are taking a risk.
What bothers us in this Party and what bothers me when I sit down with constituents is that there are those who thought that they were making an investment that was guaranteed only to find out that there was no guarantee.
I urge Hon. Members to adopt this motion and then go on to adopt other measures as well. This recommendation would require a waiver. It would require the knowledge of the people involved. It is a good motion. I urge all Hon. Members to support it.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   FINANCIAL INSTITUTIONS ADVISABILITY OF INFORMING DEPOSITORS WHEN DEPOSITS ARE UNINSURED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I too am pleased to have the opportunity to speak on this motion. As has been indicated, this motion would require financial institutions or those involved in taking deposits to have a form available which an individual would have to sign if a deposit is not to be covered by CDIC or an equivalent institution. It is obviously an attempt to increase consumer protection and to prevent people from being misled, either intentionally or unintentionally. I certainly support those goals. I think they are laudable.
In light of the fact that on the Finance Committee we have been dealing recently with the issue of bank service charges
April 25, 1988

and the disclosure provisions around them we have had some interesting evidence about just how much people are aware of when they give their money to banks or trust companies. I would like to see a lot more education of consumers about what is involved in the whole financial area so that they can make those types of decisions with a more informed approach.
However, the proposal of the Hon. Member requires some further consideration to ascertain whether or not it is practically feasible. One of my concerns is whether it would imply, for example, that, if one had not signed a waiver, one's deposit would be covered automatically by CDIC or an equivalent institution at the provincial level. As the Hon. Member for Kamloops-Shuswap (Mr. Riis) pointed out in his speech, there are a number of types of deposits which are not covered. A great many people might be surprised to learn that, for example, foreign currency accounts are not covered by CDIC. The contents of one's safety deposit box and investment products with terms of more than five years, including certificates one may buy from a bank or a trust company, are not covered. Stocks, bonds, mutual funds and deposits in excess of $60,000 are not covered.
There are some practical problems that I am not sure of in each of these cases of a person signing a waiver stating that, for example, they are aware that, because they had $63,000, the additional $3,000 would not be covered by CDIC. We could get ourselves into a sort of bureaucratic morass.
We have to look at another fundamental matter. How far should we go as a Government to protect people? Again, I come back to the importance of education and increased awareness. I do not think we can legislate perfect protection for everyone. There is an important role for the Government in consumer protection. Through CDIC we are doing a great deal of work, as well as through present legislation and regulation. But we cannot take over the responsibility of an individual to make decisions and to live with the results.
The Government itself cannot ensure that there is no fraud, no attempt to mislead or to conceal. There is a limit, I am positive, to how far we should go in writing laws that so circumscribe us that our personal responsibility begins to be eroded.
As well, we must look at what is already in legislation, for example, through Bill C-42 which was debated in the House last year. Even prior to the reforms presented in Bill C-42 there was a prohibition against anyone other than a member of the Canadian Deposit Insurance Corporation representing itself as being insured by the CDIC. It would be against the law for anyone to imply that they were covered when they were not.
As you will recall, Mr. Speaker, Bill C-42 added three other provisions dealing specifically with this kind of issue. The first provision deals with the question about the extent of the existing ban on unauthorized representations of insured status of member institutions or deposits received by them. It is now
Financial Institutions
clear that this ban applies both to the institution and to all persons acting as its agents.
The second element of the Bill dealt with the provision that had been in the regulations but it was brought back in to legislation to give it real clout. It is a requirement that institutions which accept deposits not insured by CDIC indicate it clearly and distinctly in writing in the deposit contract. I know that it has been brought to the attention of the House from time to time that perhaps the writing is too small or that there is just a stamp on the back of the contract indicating that it is not covered by CDIC. Perhaps we need to look at this to make sure that the writing, the information to the consumer, is made more clear on the face of the contract so that it is something that a person cannot miss.
The third element in Bill C-42 was a new requirement which makes it an obligation for financial institutions seeking investment funds on behalf of their own security subsidiaries or other institutions which are not members of the CDIC to notify expressly the depositors that these corporations or subsidiaries are not members of CDIC, therefore, the funds invested are not insured by the CDIC. This is quite clear and very consistent with what the Hon. Member is attempting to achieve in his motion.
Having sat through the Finance Committee hearings recently with respect to the provisions of "expressly notify" or "express notice" in the Bank Act, I have some reservations about the meaning of those words. It may be that we have to revisit Bill C-42 at some time to see how the words in that Bill are being interpreted. I hope they are not being interpreted as loosely as the words under the Bank Act have been interpreted with respect to the consumer and the prices that the consumer is having to pay for bank services charges.
We have those provisions. They are new provisions, and perhaps we should give them some time to work and see if they are working. We must not forget that we did not deal with Bill C-42 in isolation last summer. We considered it in tandem with Bill C-56, and provisions in that legislation will also protect consumers, this time in an area where people are not making conventional deposits, but are in effect using depositlike instruments. Bill C-56 will make it easier to create protection plans in the insurance industry. That industry has become more and more involved in these deposit-like instruments.
The Government has been working with representatives of the industry to develop annuity and policy holder protection plans along the lines of the CDIC protection, in order that this type of thing can be extended in the future.
There may indeed still be room for confusion on the part of depositors. It is appropriate that the Government ensure that their interests are well served. Confusion will only arise, and depositors' interests will only be in danger in certain circumstances. The Government's proposals for reform of the trust

April 25, 1988
Financial Institutions
and loans companies legislation which were released last December make clear that the supervisory authority will be vigilant to protect conflicts of interest or the unclear auditor's function, and the other factors which would allow a company to deliberately mislead or confuse.
There is a larger dimension to this question. If we are creating a new type of financial sector, as we are with the changes in deregulation with new instruments and a new combination of services, then we need a new type of supervisory authority. To a large degree, this need is also being met at the federal level under the various pieces of legislation that have been and are being presented.
There is a great deal of work going on in this whole field to ensure the interests of the consumers and to work with the provinces. As my colleague, the Hon. Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn) pointed out, we have to work very closely with the provinces and try to see as much as possible that our provisions are in concert, so that people are not further confused because one group is under federal jurisdiction and living by one set of rules, and another group of financial institutions is under provincial jurisdiction with a different set of rules. We should also be working towards a more co-ordinated effort in this respect.
I believe that the intent of the motion of my colleague is very meritorious. It certainly deserves our full examination. But we should be cautious to ensure that any new provisions do not add unnecessarily to the bureaucratization and the potential confusion on the part of the consumer.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   FINANCIAL INSTITUTIONS ADVISABILITY OF INFORMING DEPOSITORS WHEN DEPOSITS ARE UNINSURED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity to participate in this debate this afternoon on the motion presented to us by my colleague, the Hon. Member for Kamloops-Shuswap (Mr. Riis). I differ in opinion with the Member who spoke to us moments ago. The Hon. Member indicated that she did not feel that this was an appropriate resolution, or one that we should be considering favourably. She also indicated, if I can paraphrase what the Hon. Member said, that perhaps this would be difficult to administer in terms of forms and so on.
I have received letters from constituents who invested in the Principal Group of companies. I have one such letter here, and I will not disclose who signed it because I have not consulted with my elector. It is important that the House and all Canadians know of some of the hardships created.
This letter states: "A television news clip on an exchange in the House of Commons yesterday regarding income taxes charged to the losers in Principal Group prompted my writing you today. I was an investor with the Principal Group of companies. On June 30, 1987 when the Treasury Department of Alberta revoked the licences of two of their subsidiaries, I held eight guaranteed term certificates and fixed term certificates with First Investors Corporation. The total Principal amount deposited with FIC was $95,000. My total evaluated claim on June 30 was $100,000 which included
interest owing to that date and calculated by Coopers & Lybrand, court appointed managers of FIC. I have received $30,000 which represents 30 per cent payment on the total claim. To date I have lost $70,000".
The voter goes on to describe the income tax provisions which have since been corrected, or at least we are led to believe have been corrected for the time being.
The purpose of my raising this letter is to indicate that all of us in the House have been affected, or have constituents who have been affected by the failure of the Principal Group of companies. This leads us to conclude, I would hope, that we have to change the ways of doing business of the financial institutions in order that Canadians are made aware of just what it is that they are investing in.
Today, I had someone pick up leaflets from various financial institutions concerning investment vehicles. I have one here from the Bank of Nova Scotia. That bank advertises its investment certificates. This leaflet states:
With a minimum investment of $5,000 GICs are available in $100 increments for terms of: 1-10 years with interest paid monthly, semi-annually or annually.
This is under the grand title of "Guaranteed Investment Certificates". The banks may call some of those investment certificates "guaranteed", but the word "guaranteed" does not really mean much. For instance, according to this suggestion if someone were to invest for 10 years, I would suggest that the guarantee has nothing to do with the Canada Deposit Insurance guarantee. In fact, it is a verbal or written guarantee or otherwise a guarantee of the financial institutions, which says, "We guarantee this to you". I do not know how valid that guarantee is. It depends on the financial viability of the financial institution in question. I suppose in some cases, it is a little like saying "cross my heart", and in other cases it probably has values which are a little more tangible.
I have another leaflet from the Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce which states, "Get us working for you! with the CIBC GIC". There is a little mark beside GIC and an explanation in fine print, because GIC stands for guaranteed investment certificate, and it states, "CIBC guaranteed investment certificates (CIBC GIC's) are issued by CIBC Mortgage Corporation and unconditionally guaranteed by Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce". If one reads the fine print, one finds that it is not guaranteed by the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation. It is only guaranteed by the bank itself. Canadians are not always given all the information.
I have another one here from VG National Trust. This is the only document which I have secured today, which actually
says:
A risk-free, secure investment backed by one of the largest trust companies in Canada and also covered by Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation (CDIC). Debentures, that are the same as GICs, provide an additional $60,000 CDIC protection.
April 25, 1988

This document talks about Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation protection because, of course, that is what they are offering. The other investment which I described a while ago in the Scotia Bank, and the one from the CBIC Mortgage Corporation, did not refer to that.
Yet, when you enter the doors of any of those financial institutions you see displayed very prominently, usually right on the door, "Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation Member" and so on. Canadians think that investments they make there are automatically covered. When they buy a guaranteed investment certificate in a place insured by the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation they naturally assume that that guaranteed investment certificate is guaranteed by the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation, which is advertised there. However, that is not so. I have just given examples of where that is not necessarily the case.
There is certainly a need for that which the Hon. Member for Kamloops-Shuswap is proposing to us. Any investment made in an institution covered by the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation which is not thereby covered should indicate such by way of waiver. The Hon. Member for Capilano (Mrs. Collins) said that this would be difficult to administer. If you have ever rented a car you will have noticed that if you decide not to buy the insurance you must sign the form indicating that you waive the privilege of having insurance. That is pre-printed on the form.
Similarly, when you buy an investment vehicle in an institution covered by CDIC there should be a pre-printed area on the forms for the constituent to initial his recognition that the particular investment he is purchasing is not covered by the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation, be it a six-year term deposit, a so-called guaranteed investment certificate in a mortgage subsidiary of the banking institution, or any other investment vehicle.
All banks are covered by CDIC, but trust companies and other corporations which advertise that they are covered by CDIC, should be required to provide a waiver in the manner proposed by the Member for Kamloops-Shuswap.
I am not going to propose an amendment to this motion, Mr. Speaker, but it should be obvious that we are only talking about financial institutions with which the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation does business. In other words, within the CDIC institutions any investment vehicles which are not covered by the CDIC should include that waiver form.
I hope Hon. Members will give their support to this motion presented to us by the Member for Kamloops-Shuswap.

Mr. Speaker, as some of my colleagues have already done and as others will before the end of this debate, I wish to thank the Leader of the New Demo-cractic Party for providing us with an opportunity to address the issue of consumer protection in their dealings with
Financial Institutions
financial institutions in Canada. This issue is of major concern to us, as Members of the Progressive Conservative Party.
I agree with the Hon. Member that it would be preferable for financial institutions to better inform their customers of deposit insurance schemes available to them. But, as it has already been stated, our Government is taking steps to reach exactly the same goals as those of the motion moved by the NDP Leader.
I suggest also that the measure contemplated in the motion or a similar motion deserves to be examined thoroughly and responsibly by financial institutions regulatory authorities on both levels of Government. It should be emphasized, however, that these authorities should also take into account several points which could make the implementation of such a measure more complicated. I will explain. Before we can insist on institutions informing customers that a deposit is not insurable, we should see how difficult it might be for an institution to identify such a deposit.
Let us consider now the case of an institution which is a member of the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation, the so-called CDIC. Deposits over $60,000 made by private individuals, or deposits automatically excluded from the definition of insurable deposit under another provision of the act, such as foreign currency deposits or others whose term exceeds five years, are not really a problem at this time. But what happens in the case of a customer who has several accounts, particularly if such accounts have been opened in different branches of the same institution? Then it is much more difficult for the institution to determine whether the total of these deposits exceeds $60,000.
It is also necessary to provide a more specific definition of the words "insurable deposits" because there are many deposit insurance organizations including, for example: the system set up pursuant to the federal legislation governing the CDIC; Quebec's Regie de l'assurance-depots which, like the CDIC, covers deposits in trust and loans companies and caisses populaires; the Corporation de fonds de securite de la confederation Desjardins, for instance, which also insures deposits in caisses populaires throughout Quebec; there are various stabilization funds and various investment and deposit insurance companies offering similar coverage in credit unions or caisses populaires in other provinces; the new compensation systems for people covered under pension schemes or life and general insurance policies.
Deposit insurance plans therefore vary from one institution to the next, be it a bank, a caisse populaire, an insurance company or what have you, just as they do depending on the government level, either federal or provincial. This has to be taken into consideration.
In addition, with the development of sales network agreements for financial products throughout the entire financial sector as provided for in the Government's new policy, financial institutions will soon be able to offer their clients a wider range of deposit and investment instruments. It could be

for example instruments delivered by institutions covered by a different insurer.
Therefore, the universal requirement that depositors be informed of their uninsured deposits should not be limited to individual deposits and investments not covered by CDIC. Several options should be examined, for example requiring the institution to indicate the insurer's name on all deposit instruments or to inform depositors or investors only if their deposit or investment is not covered by any of the previously mentioned institutions.
To avoid any confusion, I believe that it would be advisable that all plans have similar insurability standards, specially with regard to the definition of insurable deposits and limits of insurability. It would also be necessary to make sure that the various deposit insurance plans be sufficiently guaranteed in order that all depositors really be afforded comparable protection.
The legislation which is now before the House is indeed desirable, but its implementation raises the difficulties which I have indicated. However, I urge federal as well as provincial regulatory authorities to work together in resolving these difficulties and improving the information available to consumers on deposit insurance.

Mr. Speaker, thank you for giving me the opportunity to speak to this motion this afternoon. I would like to congratulate the Hon. Member for Kamloops-Shuswap (Mr. Riis) for bringing this motion to the attention of the House. It is a subject which is of great concern to all of us.
As you know, the reform of the financial sector has been an important part of this Government's economic agenda for the last three years. We have more legislation still to come and we have passed a great deal already. We attach importance to consumer protection because of the events of the last two years when many financial institutions were in some difficulty. People are concerned now about the safety of their deposits and their investments in some of these institutions. One such incident about which we have heard spoken in this Chamber today, very much in the minds of Members, is what is called the Principal Group affair. Unlike other incidents in which the federal Government was clearly involved, the Principal Group is a provincial matter. We must be careful to avoid jurisdictional problems where there is a provincial responsibility, and the federal Government would do well to follow what the province wants in some of these matters.
As I have said earlier, we have done a great deal over the last three years to strengthen financial institution management. For example, for some time now there has been a prohibition against anyone or any institution, other than a member of the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation, representing itself as being insured by the CDIC. Except in
cases of outright fraud or deliberate misrepresentation, this rule goes a long way toward protecting consumers.
There has also been a long-standing CDIC requirement that uninsured deposit instruments offered by CDIC member institutions must be clearly stamped as such. In addition, the new provision added to the CDIC Act by Bill C-42 allows institutions and their agents to indicate that deposits are insured. Taken together with other matters, these provisions would seem, at least to me, to allow the CDIC to introduce measures very similar to the one being proposed to us today.
Bills C-42 and C-56 passed and proclaimed last July clarified and strengthened many of the consumer protections in the existing law. For example, the requirement to indicate in writing on the contract that a deposit is not insured under CDIC became part of the Act itself rather than simply part of the CDIC by law.
Because other people in this Chamber want to speak to this motion this afternoon, let me come to the part that disturbs me most of all. I say again that I concur with the spirit of the motion. I do not, however, think that we can accept the motion as it now stands. It has implications for legislation relating to financial institutions. Even the complexities of these were outlined by the Hon. Member who introduced the motion himself on February 29, 1988. If one reads his comments, as recorded at page 13240 of Hansard, they are enough to cause each of us to pause and think again. The Liberal Member who spoke a few moments ago said that he wished he could amend this motion. Why, Mr. Speaker? So that we would know what institutions we were really talking about.
If we have that kind of confusion, and again looking at the comments made by the Hon. Member from Kamloops- Shuswap, recorded as I said on page 13240 of Hansard, what we have here is a motion that purports to make something simple which, in fact, is a very complex matter. Entering into negotiations with the provinces is not the way we should be heading. We should first be asking what institutions we are trying to control in this way, what kind of investments, insurance and other matters. Then we should decide where to take it.
I cannot support this motion, despite approval in the sense of what I know the Hon. Member wants, because it leads us into a complexity which I think is masked by the simplicity of the motion.
